summary: Festus succeeds Felix and quickly visits Jerusalem, where leading priests ask him to transfer Paul while planning an ambush. Festus instead summons accusers to Caesarea. They bring serious but unproved charges; Paul denies offenses against Jewish law, the temple, and Caesar. When Festus asks whether he will stand trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, invoking his right as a Roman citizen. King Agrippa II and Bernice later visit. Festus explains that the dispute concerns Jewish religion and a dead Jesus whom Paul says lives, admits he is at a loss how to investigate, and arranges a ceremonial hearing because sending a prisoner to the emperor without intelligible charges is unreasonable.
whyItMatters: Paul's appeal is neither worship of empire nor simple trust in Roman fairness; it is a legal move inside a compromised process where political favor could return him to a murder plot. Festus's summary unintentionally identifies the case's theological center—the claim that Jesus lives—while his inability to formulate a criminal charge exposes the mismatch between gospel controversy and imperial prosecution.

keyVerses.text: For if I have done wrong and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
keyVerses.why: Paul accepts genuine legal accountability while refusing politically convenient surrender to unsupported charges.

keyVerses.text: I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him.
keyVerses.why: Festus states a due-process ideal that the narrative invites readers to compare with Roman practice.

keyVerses.text: For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.”
keyVerses.why: The chapter ends with imperial administration unable to say what crime its long-held prisoner committed.

questions.question: Why do the leaders request a Jerusalem trial?
questions.answer: They present transfer as a favor from the new governor while secretly preparing an ambush. Festus refuses the requested venue and tells able accusers to come to Caesarea, where he will sit in judgment. The contrast shows how administrative procedure can temporarily interrupt lethal collusion.

questions.question: What is the ‘judgment seat’?
questions.answer: Bēma is a raised tribunal platform where the governor issues judicial decisions. Festus sits on it in Caesarea, making the hearing an exercise of Roman authority rather than informal discussion. Paul is surrounded by accusers but the narrator repeatedly says they cannot prove the serious charges.

questions.question: Why does Festus suggest Jerusalem after rejecting the first request?
questions.answer: Acts says Festus wants to gain favor with Judean leaders, so he asks Paul whether he is willing to stand trial there under Festus. The question technically preserves consent but places the prisoner under political pressure and near the planned ambush. Paul's appeal removes the governor's discretion.

questions.question: What did ‘I appeal to Caesar’ legally do?
questions.answer: A Roman citizen facing a capital case could provocatio or appeal for imperial adjudication, though exact first-century procedure is reconstructed from scattered evidence. Festus consults his council and declares, ‘To Caesar you shall go.’ Paul has not appealed because Caesar is morally superior; he has used citizenship to avoid an unsafe local transfer and secure the route to Rome.

questions.question: Who are Agrippa and Bernice?
questions.answer: Herod Agrippa II is Agrippa I's son and a Roman-aligned client king knowledgeable about Jewish affairs. Bernice is his sister, later known for a relationship with Titus; ancient rumors of incest surrounded the siblings, though Acts does not repeat them. Festus seeks Agrippa's expertise in framing the religious case.

questions.question: What does Festus mean by ‘their own religion’?
questions.answer: Deisidaimonia can mean religion, religious observance, or superstition, carrying the same ambiguity as related language in Acts 17. Festus reduces the case to disputes about Jewish religion and ‘one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.’ His outsider summary is incomplete but isolates resurrection as the issue he cannot translate into Roman criminal categories.

questions.question: Why is the hearing staged with so much pomp?
questions.answer: Agrippa and Bernice enter with phantasia—display, pageantry, or great pomp—alongside commanders and city elites. A chained prisoner is placed before imperial grandeur, yet Festus announces that crowds demand death while he has found nothing deserving it. Luke's irony makes the powerful depend on Paul to give their spectacle intelligible content.

questions.question: Why does Festus call Caesar ‘my lord’?
questions.answer: Kyrios, ‘lord,’ is ordinary for a master or sovereign and here refers to the emperor as Festus's superior. In Acts the same title most densely identifies Jesus, creating a political-theological resonance without requiring every use to mean divinity. Paul is sent to the imperial ‘lord’ because he testifies to another Lord.

questions.question: Does Roman due process prove Rome is just?
questions.answer: Festus articulates face-to-face accusation and defense as Roman custom, refuses the first transfer, and finds no capital offense. Yet Felix kept Paul for favor, Festus again courts favor, and an unconvicted man remains imprisoned without clear charges. Acts presents useful legal norms inside an empire whose officials apply them selectively.
